definition: Bequeath means to leave something to someone through a will.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word bequeath. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know bequeath should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The comedian bequeathed his notebooks to the colleague who had opened for him for thirty years, with instructions to steal only the best jokes.
Give is far less formal than bequeath — a sandwich or a pencil changes hands with no paperwork and no waiting, while a bequeathed gift needs a will, a signature, and a reading to arrive.
To hand something down goes further than to give it — a younger generation is implied — but it can happen at any birthday, while bequeath waits for the reading of a will.

Leave is the plain-speech verb a will uses — she left the house to her niece — and it works just as well for a coat left on a train. Bequeath is the formal, legal version: it only ever means a transfer written into a will, delivered after the giver's death.

To endow is to give an institution a permanent fund — a chair, a lecture series, a hospital wing — and a living giver can endow and then watch the money work. Bequeath moves a gift on paper, effective only at death: endowments are about ongoing income, a bequest about the final handover.

Donating is giving to a cause or charity — money, blood, canned goods — usually while the giver is alive to sign the form. Bequeath is personal and posthumous: property named in a will, passing to a chosen person or institution only at the giver's death.

The Old English verb cwethan, 'to say,' died out of daily speech centuries ago — only the storybook 'quoth' and the legal noun bequest keep its shape. Bequeath is a fossil: a word for saying who gets what, outliving the verb it was built on.
Bequeath means to leave something to someone through a will.
Old Marta the blacksmith let her apprentice borrow the good anvil but never gave it away.

The forge, the tongs, the anvil, and the little book of hammer notes stayed hers until her will was read; she had bequeathed all of it, exactly as she put it in writing, to the apprentice who had swept her floor for nine years.
Bequeath is the exact word for what Marta did, because it means to leave something to someone through a will — the handover waits for the will to be read.
Hand down comes close, but a grandmother can hand down a ring on any birthday; bequeath keeps the lawyer, the paper, and the waiting in the picture.
Bequeath belongs to wills: it is how a benefactor gives one final time, on paper, effective at death.
For a ring passed across the dinner table, hand down is the honest word; keep bequeath for the lawyer's office.
Largess and munificence, its unit-mates, describe giving the giver is alive to enjoy.

The letter from the mainland law office reached the island on the same boat as the flour.
Astrid Larsen, who had kept the light for forty-one years, had died in the spring; her will, the letter said, was short.
She chose to bequeath her whole library — nine hundred books, hauled out one crate a summer — to the island's one-room school.
There were conditions, in the careful language wills use: the books could never be sold, and the shelf by the window must stay reserved for whoever kept the light after her.
The teacher read the letter twice, then began, that same afternoon, to clear a wall.
